utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Obviously, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his urgent matters. He will join us tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I just wanted to raise a couple of matters in connection with Mr. Robinson's submissions yesterday. Let me make it clear from the outset, I'm not attempting in any way to revisit the Court's decision, but simply to clarify some matters on the record so the record is as clear as possible. First, with respect to the submissions in support of the motion for additional time, Mr. Robinson mentioned the credibility of General Smith and appeared to represent that the general had stated that: "They had no capability to use laser-guided weapons for the air-strikes." Although it's not entirely clear who is meant by "they" in that reference, we were unable, in any event, to find support for that submission in General Smith's evidence and would, at least, request an appropriate transcript cite or a correction in respect of that. Secondly, with respect to the submission that a notation in Mr. Banbury's notebook would be the "first confirmation" that there was, on the UN side, negotiations for exchange, I note that while it's somewhat unclear, what was meant by "first confirmation," it certainly suggests that the information was new or unique, and in that regard I would direct the Trial Chamber to the cross-examination of General Smith at transcript pages 11891 to 11894 on the 15th of February, where the accused cross-examined and received information on that very issue. And, finally, Mr. President, with respect to the submissions suggesting that the problem with getting to these particular questions that are the subject of today's extended hearing were the responsibility or the fault of the Court's allocation of time, we would reject that characterisation. The review of the record, we believe, demonstrates that those matters could have been embraced within the time allotted easily, with a focused cross-examination, without argumentation or commentary, et cetera, and the responsibility lies with the accused. Those are the points I wanted to raise. Thank you for your time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Taking this opportunity of the witness being absent: After this witness, we'll be resuming to hear Mr. Prstojevic's remaining examination-in-chief. For the planning purpose, can I hear from you? How long would you take for your remainder of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My expectation is to complete it within one session, if not sooner; that is, an hour-and-a-half session. And I will actually be making -- or raising a point in that regard to facilitate the process, I trust. But as the Court is aware, projecting time-periods in this instance is a little more difficult than it normally is, but that's my hope and expectation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't wish to oppose respected Mr. Tieger, but just the fact the notes were written by hand and I had to ask Mr. Robinson, as an American, to try to decipher it, I am not able to read, and it's a huge amount. If the OTP had transcribed it, if we had it typed out, I would have studied it in time, and probably there would be other elements that would be significant. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, now, Mr. Tieger did say that this would not be a revisiting of the Court's decision, but we should like very much to hear you on his submission this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Judge Baird. I was feeling uneasy myself when the Prosecutor sometimes says that I mischaracterised the record and then we just move on. So I would like to call your attention to, first of all, on the transcript of the 15th of January, 2011, page 11880, where General Smith said there were no forward air controllers involved in the attacks carried out in May, which is what I was referring to when we talked about the laser-guided bombs. Secondly, with respect to the exchange of prisoners, on the 15th of February, at page 11894, General Smith said that he thinks that there was an exchange, but he wasn't involved, essentially, in the negotiations, which is true, because that was being done by General Janvier, who was working directly with Mr. Banbury in Zagreb at the time. So those are the two references for the points that I made, and I stand by my submissions that I made yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber wants to make sure that the allowance for additional time was granted on an exceptional basis, and this should not be interpreted as a precedent. And, finally, for planning purposes, the Chamber will sit on Monday next week. And thanks to the Tolimir Bench, we'll be able to sit in an extended format, i.e., from 9.00 to 2.30. Let's bring in the witness. Mr. Karadzic, you'll have about half an hour, and the subject-matter is to be limited to the issues relating to his notes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banbury. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Banbury. I would like to ask you something, as briefly as possible, which concerns your notes. Firstly, could you tell me, as I know that you are being promoted now along the UN lines, but at the time when you were making these notes, what was your role? Was your role to note this truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of my roles was to attend meetings that my superiors were attending as the principal, and I was there to essentially record what had transpired and then to draft a report to either UNPROFOR headquarters -- normally, UNPROFOR headquarters, recounting the event, the meeting, what the exchanges had been, and then to provide an assessment of the meaning or significance of the exchange that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take part in the talks?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, and perhaps more so as time went on and my superiors became more knowledgeable of my role or my contributions. I perhaps spoke up a little bit more. But normally, my role was to be silent, but sometimes I spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you change anything that was said or did you record everything as truthfully as possible?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recorded everything as truthfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see in e-court 1D3476.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the 12th notebook, book 12 of your note-books, which begins on the 17th of May, which deals with the month of May 1995 through to the 10th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see page 29 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please identify the participants of this meeting held on the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the deputy force commander, the NATO liaison officer, Colonel Rudd, John Almstrom -- "J.G." is probably Jack Greenberg, Emma Shitaka, who was a political affairs officer, Chris Gunnas [phoen], who worked in the spokesman's office, myself, "A.B.," together with the SRSG -- sorry, together with the SRSG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please continue and explain to us what you recorded in the following five or six lines? Can you just explain to us what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been a discussion on the situation of Sarajevo, a question of whether air-strikes were appropriate. Seven Bosnian military and eighteen Bosnian Serb Army confirmed violations of the heavy weapons exclusion zone. The SRSG said: "Maybe hit them at the ratio of 3:1." I suppose he was referring there to air-strikes against both the Bosnian Serb Army and the Bosnian Government: "Three weapons collection points were being used by the Bosnian Serb Army in today's shellings; i.e., weapons -- heavy weapons from the UN-monitored weapons collection points within the 20-kilometre heavy weapons exclusion zone were being used by the Bosnian Serb Army to participate in the shelling. "Smith was thinking that we would strike tomorrow, we'll use laser-guided bombs." Four weapons are loose from the weapons collections point -- four weapons have been taken out of the weapons collections points and presumably were beyond UNPROFOR's monitoring at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And "Smith," that is Admiral Smith; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, yes, Admiral Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to explain the penultimate line for us, because I think one of the words has not been recorded. [In English] "Laser-guided bomb"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, I can't read my own writing there. I don't know what kind of bombs. "Laser-guided --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would it be "smart bombs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's probably what it is. Yes, sir, "smart bombs," "laser-guided smart bombs." Yes, that's probably what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see page 33 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the following sentence. The first, second -- the sixth line from above, the special representative of the Secretary-General. If you can just explain to us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's, again, an internal meeting with the SRSG, the deputy force commander, the NATO liaison officer, the chief of staff, John Almstrom, Jack Greenberg, Emma Shitaka. "Fred" was probably Fred Eckhart from the spokesman's office, and myself. And the SRSG starts off by saying: "Albright," that is to say, Madeleine Albright, who at the time, I guess, would have -- I don't know if she was the -- still the ambassador to the UN or the secretary of state, probably the ambassador to the UN of the United States: "Albright was upset at our intention to strike the Bosnian Government. We never had such an intention. We were prepared to, if necessary, violations, but we don't equate the actions of the sides."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I read this "Albright upset"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Albright upset."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Over" or what?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At our --" that's my symbol for "@," like the e-mail address: "Albright upset @ our intention to strike Bosnian Government military forces."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you need the previous page in order to identify the meeting? Can we please have a look at page 40 so that Mr. Banbury could see what this is all about, because this is the continuation of what precedes. Can you just tell us what meeting this was?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this picks up still in the middle of the meeting. And that's not the first page of the notes from that meeting, I don't believe, so I'm not sure which meeting it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there several meetings held on the 27th of May or was this the only one?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, off-hand. There quite possibly were several. Again, I would need to -- to flip through. There it is, that's the beginning of the meeting there. Okay, 27 May, 8.30 in the morning. The SRSG is meeting with the SRSG, the force commander, the deputy force commander, the chief of staff, the NATO liaison officer, John Almstrom, Jack Greenberg, a Dutch colonel, probably from the chief of staff's office, the force commander's aid, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still need this introduction, the opening words of the SRSG?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need it, no. If you'd like me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please, just the first statement of the SRSG. This is Mr. Akashi, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, this is Mr. Akashi, and he's saying that the Secretary-General went to the Security Council and had also spoken to President Chirac: "The French are anxious that better measures need to be put in place to protect UN personnel. These measures should be taken. Possibly including concentrating our troops," in other words not having them so dispersed, "and that we should perhaps focus on our mandate and take more energetic measures. Withdraw of UNPROFOR, if possible, but only if the situation becomes impossible --" "or only if the above," I'm sorry, "only if the above becomes impossible."; in other words, these measures I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, the force commander, "FC" stands for "Force Commander"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to explain for us the first sentence -- the first and second sentences, rather?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The force commander is saying: "The fundamental problem of weapons collection points was they were set up in a case of urgency. The use of the weapons - under what circumstances - was never defined. The concept of demilitarisation never took hold. The progressive erosion of the exclusion zone, the use of weapons," i.e., heavy weapons, "has led us to where we are now. Soldiers are hostages and shields against air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That reflects accurately what was said; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now, please, have a look at page 47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to be precise, that reflects accurately the sense of what was said. It's not necessarily verbatim, but it's certainly the essence of what the force commander said or others say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does that concern only this note or all of the notes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the notes. It was impossible to take absolute verbatim notes. I tried as best as possible to reflect what was said. Where there were very important statements, I tried to put even quote marks around them. So the notes reflect very accurately what was said, but it's not a verbatim record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain for us what the SRSG was saying, and the first sentence of the force commander's response: "Are talks continuing ...," and so on and so on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SRSG said: "Are talks continuing on the exchange of prisoners between us and the Bosnian Serb Army." The force commander said they -- the talks are interrupted now and that he would talk to the SRSG later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That also reflects what was being said; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have a look at page 61 now, and can we please zoom in on the upper part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was happening on the 2nd of June, when you attended?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this was a very difficult time for UNPROFOR, following the strikes at the end of May and the response by the Bosnian Serb military against us, the hostage-taking, the shelling in Tuzla and other places. So I know that this was a very difficult time. I don't recall precisely what was happening on June 2nd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see the previous page as well so that Mr. Banbury might identify this specific meeting and the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would this be of help?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the regular morning briefing of the SRSG.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see the following page, that is, page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us? "Gen," is it some general who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this -- this is referring to General Divjak, but the identification of the speaker here would be on the previous page. This is a continuation, probably, of what I was writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Fred," does that help you, "Fred"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, thank you. "Fred" would refer to Fred Eckhart from the spokesman's office.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the previous page once again, the bottom half, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it Fred who's speaking?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Fred Eckhart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Fred Eckhart says that: "In an interview for the BBC, I called these prisoners war prisoners. Karadzic holds them to be prisoners of war"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to what Fred told the meeting, that you had given an interview to the BBC, where you threatened retaliation against the UNPROFOR military personnel that we referred to as hostages. But in that interview, you referred to them as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that interview?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to my recollection. It's possible, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is that Fred Eckhart is saying, reporting?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Eckhart says that: "General Divjak said that the NATO target was very well chosen, one of the most heavily fortified military targets in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Destruction of the ammunition stocks has already had an impact on the Bosnian Serb Army attacks on Sarajevo. The Bosnian Serbs will need 15 to 30 days to replenish the stocks from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this General Jovan Divjak the general from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who said this about targets?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been the same General Divjak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, pages 29, 30, 40, 41, 47 and 61, I would like to tender them, please. If it would be helpful, then perhaps page 60 would also be acceptable because the speaker is identified in that way. I think one of them has already been exhibited by the Prosecution, but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just on that, Your Honours, especially given that Mr. Banbury has noted that these are excerpts from meetings and he has difficulty sometimes putting them in context without looking at the speakers who are on previous pages and other such things, I actually think, rather than excerpts and separate pages, it would be of greater use to everyone to have the notes from those days. Mr. Banbury has already indicated that it was an intense time, it was a difficult time, and there were often several meetings during the course of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were excerpts which relate to the whole meeting, that specific meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At a minimum, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But there are some parts you are not going to tender, even if we saw some part of it? For example, page 33, referring to Madam Albright, you're not tendering that page? I want to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly, certainly. However, 29, 33, 41, 47 and 61 -- possibly 60, and 61, unless we opt for the entire meeting or the sentences just before the meeting started. We don't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit those pages related to those five specific meetings. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit D1176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You concluded your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I have been confined to this topic, I have finished. Thank you, Mr. Banbury. Thank you, Excellencies, for this additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, reviewing the materials from yesterday and listening to today, I can indicate I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and staying with us for a long time to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll need a longer-than-normal interruption between two witnesses to both log on and log off and assemble quite a number of materials, so I'd ask for a break for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How longer than normal? Ten minutes would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 10 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Hayden. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I indicated a bit earlier that I would be seeking to facilitate the process today, and I wanted to advise the Court, generally in accordance with the practice we've followed up to now with the witness, that I would be moving more quickly in the course of this remaining examination to the use of pointed or leading questions, and I wanted to let the Court know that. This is, in our submission, appropriate for any number of reasons. First, generically, the jurisprudence of this institution, the jurisprudence of adversarial systems, recognise that there are categories of witnesses for whom the use of such techniques of examination are appropriate. Indeed, there's a rule of evidence in the United States, but I believe it's reflected in other jurisdictions in other forms, that provides that when a witness is identified with an adverse party, interrogation may be by leading questions. That's a reflection of two things, as the cases note; number 1, the fact that the Prosecution obviously takes witnesses where it finds them, and in any number of instances they will be witnesses who are -- who may be accomplices, co-conspirators, or otherwise persons who have a reason to provide evidence that is -- or to slant testimony in a manner -- in a particular manner. And, again, that's reflected in our jurisprudence as well, providing wide latitude under circumstances for efficient examination, and a reflection of the fact that under such circumstances, there is no risk of the concern that underlies leading questions, and that is that a party will simply agree to a proposition presented to him or her by an advocate with whom he or she identifies. But beyond that, of course, we have the example of this particular witness's testimony thus far. And, indeed, I suspect that the Chamber may think the use of more focused questions is long overdue, as reflected by some of the questions asked by the Bench at the end of the session when we adjourned. The witness has engaged in long, digressive responses that moved away from the focus of the question and the point of the question, often volunteering information; thought that he clearly considered to be in support of positions he wanted to advance. He actually mentioned that he'd come here to prove certain things. And perhaps most of the point -- the first two matters I want to raise involve areas where this particular witness has levelled a kind of attack on what the Prosecution said or what his position was in previous instances. Even colloquially, we have a situation where we have a hostile witness. I think -- and I think it would be, clearly, inappropriate to ask -- to treat this witness as if he is a normal, co-operative witness in the context where he's actually raised allegations that need to be addressed in that particular manner. For what it's worth, I mentioned this to Mr. Robinson as well. I don't think he has any particular objection to the use of such questions and maximising the use of our time in the remaining period we have. But, as I say, because I indicated at the outset I would attempt to move progressively through this process, and did so, that is, first posing open-ended questions to the witness and then focusing more carefully, I think we've reached a point now where we can move more expeditiously through this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection, and we think that the Chamber has to make that determination under paragraph 26 of the Popovic decision. And we think that the Prosecutor, having now made the application -- or even having made the application earlier to the Chamber that sat last week, and was indicated that he would be allowed to ask leading questions, I think these are the kind of circumstances which actually the Rule is designed for, so I don't have any objection to his doing that. I would note that your instinct to have this witness testify viva voce, as opposed to adopting wholesale the Krajisnik testimony, has proven to be a good one, since he's disowned some of his Krajisnik testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic. How are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, I'm well. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I want to take you back to where the examination was when we temporarily concluded your testimony on Friday, the 11th. And at that time, the focus of the examination was on P1492, an intercepted telephone conversation dated the 14th of June, 1992, during which, among other things, we see in the intercept the quote from you: "Well, what shall we do? Would it be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from a side outside to expel them all? Nobody needs to be shot or killed. Everybody expelled." And your interlocutor says: "That would be the right move." There's further discussion about that, but the question was then asked: "When you refer to organising people from outside to expel them all, who did you have in mind?" You provided -- or started to provide what was a fairly long answer about when the conversation was taking place, what neighbourhood you're from, how well or sparsely populated the neighbourhood was, et cetera. The Judge -- the Presiding Judge then said: "Witness, do you have a short -- or affirmative or short answer, in any event, to Mr. Tieger's question? Regardless of the surrounding circumstances, who did you mean by people from outside?" You said: "It is well known who these people are in the situation." Et cetera. Then you went on to say: "The MUP and the military police come out, run out, and they arrest all those who are military age ..." Et cetera. The Judge then asked: "Are you then saying in your answer that what you meant was that the MUP and the military police should be the people to expel them?" You then talked about the MUP -- some reference to the MUP from the western part and the military police, and then went on to say: "These people never moved out." You talked about the number of households. And then I asked you about something you had said before, directing your attention to an interview you had in 2005 concerning this very intercepted conversation, indicating that at page 41, you were asked: "When you say 'bring people from outside,' who are you thinking of? And your answer was: "For example, I think about the group of Arkan's, group of Boban, Brne's group, who is from Pale, any unit from outside." And I ask you: "That's what you said, isn't it, Mr. Prstojevic, and that's what you meant by 'people from outside?'" And your answer was: "That is not correct, I did not say that. You are totally diluted, Mr. Tieger." I take it you recall that exchange we had, Mr. Prstojevic. Is that right? Just yes or no, because I want to show you something in response to that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then, let me actually -- that interview, in fact, was recorded on videotape. That's 65 ter 22231. And for the benefit of the interpreters, we'll be looking at page 41 through page 42. I'm sorry, 65 ter 40243. First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, you recognise the people shown on screen now? This is a portion of 65 ter 40243, with the time code indicating -- well, this time code is just the very beginning of this clip. So that's -- and we'll mark it as we go through. You recognise yourself in there, Mr. Prstojevic, as well as people attending the interview?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please. I do recognise myself, and I do not recognise anyone else here. Secondly, during your introductory remarks, you said many words that were untrue, and you provided a lot of untrue information. Thirdly, if this is an interview from 2003, could you start a bit earlier, and then you will see that you got it wrong, in terms of what I'm providing as an answer, who I meant. At one moment just before that sentence, the topic of the conversation changes. I think that there is some Stjepan involved. He moves on to a completely different topic, and he asks me about paramilitary --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, we're going to play this right now. And the previous references, the Court will be able to check the transcript of these proceedings concerning the accuracy of what I said regarding what happened on Friday, March 11th. But let's look at this interview right now. And please recall that I asked you if you had said that. So let's -- first of all, let's play this first portion to make sure we're agreed that we're talking about the same intercept, P1492. If we could just begin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "This is intercept bears the numbers 0401-3878, 0401-3882, and is an intercept that was recorded on the 14th of June, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prstojevic, this 14th of June intercept, P1492, bears the ERN numbers 0401-3878, so I take it we can agree this discussion was about the intercepted telephone conversation during which you are recorded as talking about organising people from outside to expel them all. That's the same conversation that's at issue here; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that conversation. However, you are abusing this, you and your investigators. I did not say that they should be expelled. I said that they should move out. That is a completely different term, in relation to "expel." And that can be heard very well during the course of that speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, whether it should be interpreted to move out or to expel, that's a separate matter we can take care of later on, but let's concentrate on the questions put by Mr. Tieger at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could move now to -- let me show Mr. Reid. Let's see if we're in the relevant section now. If we can start to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "How many did he kill?" "I don't know what was I thinking, but, in essence, we did not bring people from outside and we did not plan to do that." "How many what?" "It's okay. Just, when you say 'bring people from outside,' who are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "For example, I think about the group of Arkan's, group of Boban, Brne's group, who is from Pale, any unit from outside. "Group of Boban, Brne's group, who is from Pale, any unit from outside."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Because we defended ourselves on the basis of our own forces, from local forces." "On the basis of our own forces which is -- forces made of local people and people who were refugees in our territory."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "But I did not hear the word 'expel.' It's not in accordance with -- it's not in accordance with my principles." "Well, it's not in accordance with my principles, with the way I think. However, I do not want to exclude that possibility. But it's not in accordance with my principles."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, as I follow the words spoken by the interpreter, the transcript on screen, and the transcript of the question I asked you on Friday, they seem to be identical. So do you now acknowledge that that -- that you were asked in 2005, when you say, Bring people from outside, who are you thinking of, and you said, for example: "I think about the group of Arkan's, the group of Boban, Brne's group, who is from Pale, any group from outside"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that. Play this back. Listen to everything I said. And Stjepan Margans [phoen], I have that here translated into Serbian, and Your Honours will understand everything, that we changed the subject. From the telephone conversation, we moved on to discussing these groups that came from elsewhere, and for two pages we are discussing these groups. We are not discussing my telephone conversation with the man from Kasindol, from the Civilian Protection there. Please, let us go back to Margan's question and then my answer, and you will you see that the subject had been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me expedite this by tendering - I take it there will be no objection - the entirety of the passage dealing with this. That covers approximately -- it's actually from 17:41 to 29:28 of this 65 ter number, and, of course, I tender it. It will be available to the Court to read -- to listen to and to consider in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have a transcript for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we now heard that the fact that this video-clip has been cut up changes the meaning. Why are we just taking the part that was challenged by the witness, and he claims that the meaning was changed in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for the Chamber to determine later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exactly, and I'm not -- I'm tendering the entirety of the discussion concerning this intercept. And if anyone identifies a further portion, I'll be happy to tender that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, in connection with the discussion that took place regarding your speech at the 17th Assembly session, that is, the Assembly session that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you move from that intercept of the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's already in evidence as P1492.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't checked. It's still in the status of MFI'd? Mr. Prstojevic, did you confirm that that is your voice? Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did confirm that. However, I have the original translation into Serbian here. The subject changed. As a matter of fact, we did hear this conversation. There's a point where I say that we did not bring people from elsewhere. In general terms, we did not, and that was heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was dealing with the intercept, itself. You confirm that that was your voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can admit it in its entirety, without having to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us move.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I was turning our attention to the 17th Assembly session and your remarks during the course of that session, which was held in July of 1992, I think specifically July -- toward the end of July, July 24th through 26th of 1992. And among -- there was discussion about what was said and what was not said in connection with that. And among the things you said at this time, at transcript pages 129240, was: "Mr. Tieger gave himself the right to say that it's one-and-the-same word, 'protjerali' and 'potisli,' that these two words mean the same thing in the Serbian language, which is completely incorrect. It is like the sky and the earth." And I'd like to address your assertion, Mr. Prstojevic, that the Prosecution asserted, in the course of the Krajisnik case, that the word "protjerali" and the word "potisli" mean the same thing and thereby misled the Chamber. Now, first of all, let me direct your attention generally to some matters that occurred during the Krajisnik case. And I'll note a number of these and ask if you recall them or can confirm them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The transcript pages that you referred to is a transcript of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In these proceedings, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have it down as -- I think I have one too many -- I think that would be 12924, but I'd have to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There was an unnecessary "0" at the end. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is the following correct, that during the course of the Krajisnik case: For example, at page 14676, you looked at the transcript and read the word as "potjerali," and indeed said that more than once; that at page 14676, the Court read the word as "potjerali," as did the booth some seven pages later; the booth confirmed that the word meant "chase away," not "push back"; that confirmation was necessary because you, in reading the transcript, had substituted the word "potisnuli," a variation of "potisli," when you were reading the text? You were later asked about that, and you said, well, the document says "potjerali," and I'm referring to page 14676, but that you would not use that word and you considered "potisnuli" an adequate term to substitute. And, finally, rather than asserting that the two words were the same, it was the Prosecution who pointed out that the two words were different, and that you had used the word "potisnuli" instead of the word "potjerali"? Isn't -- and that was at page 14681. Isn't that all correction, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what's correct. I could see from the previous part that you are proving things that are incorrect. And even here the word "pushed back" has to do with pushing back enemy units at the front backwards. And "expelling" is another word that refers to civilian population. And "potjerali," "chase away," it has to do with driving cattle, for example. "Potjecali," it has to do with chemical reactions. In documents, I can find four words, and I could only have used -- knowing how I speak and the manner of speaking, I could only have said "potisnuli," that is to say, "pushed back," and it had to do with enemy military units. And I said that this was in connection with Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you've raised -- by the way -- and, Your Honour, I'm going to move, to short-circuit this, by tendering the relevant pages of the Krajisnik testimony so the Court can see for itself exactly what was said and at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those would be -- that should start at page 14662 and conclude at 14681, but I will double-check to make sure we have the entirety of that. And, obviously, the Defence is free to indicate if there are any pages concerning that discussion that were not contained in that range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prstojevic, you also mentioned the word "potjecali," and I take it you consider that that's not -- you said it has to do with chemical reactions. I take it you consider that that is not a word that was used at the time, and if you see it in a document, it must be a typo or a mistake; is that it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The document which I have here in front of me precisely includes the word "potjecali." It cannot be a typo, because the formulation is different and the way you type this is different. It says here "potjecati."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that "potjecati" means "originate"? Now, I don't know how you get that translation back, but when I use the word "originate," it means -- I'll try to find a synonym -- which means "to begin from," for example. I'm trying to avoid a situation where we simply get translated back the same word that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, it's to originate, to encourage it, means the origin, what something comes from, but also, in chemistry, to encourage something, to cause, to bring about a chemical reaction. If you use a catalyst, then you help the chemical reaction to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also -- and that's in its -- as I understand it, in its grammatically correct form. Is it also the case that in a grammatically incorrect form, but, nevertheless, sometimes used, "potjecati" can also mean either "chase away" or "encourage"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, again, the Court is going to have the benefit of the transcript, and it has the benefit of being able to turn to highly sophisticated translation and interpretation resources to address any concerns about the meaning of particular words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you, by any chance, have before you the Krajisnik transcript page 14681?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first full submission of yours there contains some three B/C/S words. Are they correctly spelled? Are they the same words we discussed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, they should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Potjerali."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There are a number of words discussed, Your Honour, and let me see if I can answer the Court's question in this fashion: To the extent possible -- excuse me. I referred to the use of particular words during the Krajisnik case. So when you see, on page 14681, those three words, "potjerali," "protjerali," and "potisli," those are words that were mentioned during the course of the Krajisnik testimony by this witness. And I think the Court will find references to them. I can actually provide certain references right now. They will be contained in the pages of the transcript that we submitted. The word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, you used a different word?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was a word that was used by this witness during the course of this testimony, but was not -- I don't believe was raised, although the record will indicate one way or another, during the course of the Krajisnik testimony. In any event, it was not the focus of that discussion, as the Court should be able to see from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a way for the court reporters to have the exact correct spelling of the words you used today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the best thing to do -- I mean, we can provide that, Your Honour, although I can indicate there are potentially dialectic and grammatical differences, I think -- and I'll give that some thought, but I think the words will be -- at least the words used during the course of the Krajisnik case will be clear in context because they are mentioned several times. They're mentioned, as I indicated -- the word "potjerali," which has been mentioned here, was mentioned by the witness more than once. You can find that on page 14676 and other portions. It's mentioned by the Court also at that same page. The booth reads the transcript, and you'll see that same word again at 14673 through 74. And I can find further reference, if necessary, but it will be present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, we can find the words that were used in the Krajisnik trial, but what I was concerned about was the words that were used by you being different from the Krajisnik transcript, whether we can get it right or not. Could you let us know, in brief terms, what different terms you have used today, other than these three ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only additional term that I used came from this witness's testimony in this case earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you spell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was the word "projecali," and that difference is, as I understand it -- and, again, I'm relying on what appears in the transcript, what was said in court, and what I can glean from extensive discussions with interpreters. The word "potjerali" is spelled p-r-o-t-j-e-r-a-l-i [sic], and "protjecali" is a word which is p-r-o-t-j-e-c-a-l-i, so you have a C instead of the R. At least that's the way I've been using it, and that's the way I understood the distinction that was drawn by the witness, which is why, because he referenced it here, which is why I brought his attention to it and asked him a few questions about it and brought it to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I notice the time. It's time to take a break. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I have information from the Chamber's staff, who understand B/C/S, to the effect that the word spelled in the Krajisnik transcript as "potisjili," p-o-t-i-s-j-i-l-i, is misspelled and should be spelled as "potisnuli," p-o-t-i-s-n-u-l-i, which is one of the words the witness used today. And so all these should be checked again, and probably the Chamber will be benefitted having a submission or the submission from the CLSS, having --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly understand, Your Honour, and agree. I think the reference -- if I recall correctly, that both the word "potjecali" and "potisnuli" were separately used, perhaps one incorrectly in the -- or appear in the Krajisnik transcript, but I certainly understand the Court's concern and fully agree with the need to be as accurate as possible, and we'll review all the transcript for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably, the best way to deal with this is to have a submission from you, and that can be checked against by the Defence as well as by the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, I think that sounds like a very sensible expedient. And in that regard, I was going to note that I took a last portion of the transcript, when the Court asked about the additional word used. I correctly indicated earlier, I think, that it was "potjecali," beginning with p-o-t, but then I proceeded to spell it, I spelled it as p-r-o, rather than p-o-r, which is how it was intended to be, and that underscores the need, I think, to review for that purpose. In other words, not to go back to it, the witness in the Krajisnik case made a distinction between "potjerali," which is defined as "chased away," and "protjerali," which means "expel," and then in this case referred earlier to the word "potjecali," which was the subject of some discussion today as meaning "originate" and some other possible meanings. And when I tried to spell it at the end of the last session, it should have been as p-o-t, not p-r -- excuse me, p-o-r -- we're doing it again. Anyway, "potjecali" and "potjerali," were the two words that I was referring to there. But, again, I'll take your comments very much on board, and we'll be going through it and working with the Defence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn next to P -- another intercepted telephone conversation, this one dated 25 June 1992. That's P1515.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I believe you'll recognise this as a conversation which you had the opportunity to hear most recently during this visit to The Hague; specifically, on the 2nd of March of this year, and it's a conversation between you and Rade Ristic. At the beginning of the conversation, Ristic is on the phone, seeking to speak to you. You ask about the situation. Ristic says: "It's so -- not bad, but not either." You ask whether what was taken is now being kept. Ristic says: "Well, about that one thing, they are not going any further, fuck it." And you say: "All right. But have them hold on to it tightly, and have them all killed there, please." Ristic says: "Yes." You say: "All that is Muslim is to be killed, like Alija ..." Ristic says: "Yes." Then turning to the next page in the English, you say: "I don't want to see one military-aged Muslim alive there." Ristic says: "Aha." And then you say: "Secondly, immediately, I give you the authorisation to give Muslim apartments to Serbs there." Ristic says: "Where?" You say: "Well, there, in that part of Dobrinja." Mr. Prstojevic, can you confirm that you listened to this intercept, as I say, most recently, if not before, on the 2nd of March, and confirm that this was your voice in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the discussion between you and Mr. Ristic is about a portion of Sarajevo that has already been taken by the Bosnian Serbs, right, and that you want to ensure is held on to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is a conversation between myself and Mr. Rade Ristic, who is involved in civilian affairs of the Gojkovic local community or the area of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. I'm speaking with a civilian, who is not a commander of any sort and who was practically dealing with security, and I am being informed -- this is during the June Muslim offensive that lasted for 50 days. We managed to repel it, and we took Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV under our control. Everything that is said here refers to that part, and this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender P1515 not for MFI any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My record shows that it's fully admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what I had indicated as well, but in light of the previous discussion -- yeah, that's fine. Thank you. If we could turn next to 65 ter 31709.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I think you'll recognise this as a -- this is a conversation that is dated as the 10th of July, 1995, between you and Mr. Tepavcevic. It's a conversation that I believe you had an opportunity to listen to when you listened to a number of intercepts in 2005, which was the same interview we looked at a bit earlier, and I think you'll recognise that from the discussion in the transcript. It begins with greetings between Tepavcevic and someone from Ilidza municipality, looking for Rade Ristic, and then you come on the phone. There is greetings between you and Tepavcevic, a discussion about what the soldiers are doing, and whether everything is all right. Further discussion continues about what activities are underway, what has not been happening, as we see in the second page of the English and the second page of the B/C/S: "Nothing in the last two or three days." And if we turn to the third page of the English, the conversation continues about -- first it begins that: "They," presumably there had been reference to the Turks, "are probably up to something. They attacked an unprotected zone in Sarajevo. When we attacked them, then everybody is --" Tepavcevic says: "Yes, we've heard all that." You say: "Whining." He says: "Yes." You say: "They whine as loud as they can." Tepavcevic: "That's what they always do." You say: "Yes, yes." Tepavcevic says: "May they whine their entire lives." You say: "When they disappear, they won't whine anymore." And Tepavcevic says: "With God's help." First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, by looking at the transcript, can you confirm this is a conversation you've had a chance to listen to before and that you recognised your voices, a participant in that discussion?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the -- first of all, when you refer to "they disappearing," are you referring to those you called Turks in the earlier part of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. Here, I am speaking during the June offensive in 1995 aimed at the east part of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, with a person from the Civilian Protection who is unfit for service and did not serve his military term of duty. The entire conversation has to do with civilian defence and what they did, and we were just joking, the two of us. And you can see from the conversation that they did certain -- put up certain protections in the neighbourhood where there was Muslim sniper activity at the civilian population. They were helping the Serbian soldiers to order certain defensive lines, and I was simply joking with this person who wasn't being asked for anything in that local commune, but was heading the civilian defence. And I, incidentally, informed him that in the western sector, the Muslim offensive had not succeeded. We had beaten them. This offensive took 45 days at Serbian Sarajevo and at some parts of Treskavica and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender for admission 65 ter 31709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2514, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, during the course of some questions about the 17th Assembly session, there was a discussion about Sarajevo and the division of Sarajevo; that is, raised some questions in connection with that, and you said that when you were speaking in July of 1992, you weren't thinking about the strategic objectives then. I think you said that at 13247. When do you say, if at all, you found out that Sarajevo was part of the strategic objectives and that there was an effort underway for the division of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said on a number of occasions that I found out about the strategic objectives when they were published in the "Official Gazette" of Republika Srpska and when we received them. Until then, everything that we did was on our own initiative, and we did it on the basis of self-organising in order to defend our ethnic territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you periodically hear references, particularly references by the Bosnian Serb leadership -- let me step back for a second. Did you understand that the division of Sarajevo meant the division of Sarajevo into two cities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely this was our desire, the wish of the Serbian population in Sarajevo, and this is what we wanted, ultimately. We constantly asked our leadership to provide guarantees to us that this area would not be handed over to the Muslims in some peace process. However, as you can see, pursuant to the Dayton Accords, the main part of it, 90 per cent of the urban area, was handed over, and 10 per cent remained as part of Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you hear from members of the Bosnian Serb leadership that pursuant to the strategic aims or objectives adopted by the Assembly, that Sarajevo would be turned into two cities if -- based on that Bosnian Serb aim?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was understood that I did hear of it, because citizens kept constantly asking me whether Ilidza would be handed over, what would happen with other parts of Serbian Sarajevo. Then we, in turn, asked, and then -- starting from ministers, or any other functionaries, up to President Karadzic, if we had the opportunity. And naturally we always received assurances that everything would be done, that Serbian Sarajevo would remain, as a whole, where our ethnic area is. However, we all know what happened later in Dayton. Of course, I heard about it, and I did tell people that there would be a split in two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you to look quickly at 65 ter 45177. This is a videotape, you'll see, Mr. Prstojevic, not -- that is not in colour, of a meeting held in 1995. And if we could go quickly to approximately 1:43:30, and play that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could stop quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, do you recognise yourself present and speaking at that meeting, and did you hear the reference to you by the commentator?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but something is odd here. At the time, I was wearing a military uniform and boots, but probably that day I changed into my suit, into civilian clothing, to be adequately or appropriately dressed at this meeting. But, yes, it is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as the camera canvassed the group at the table, did you recognise any of the persons present?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised -- perhaps you can bring back or go back a little bit. I did recognise some people, but I couldn't tell you now. I think all of the people should have been familiar to me. This is Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the Assembly. And there are some people here from the municipality of Ilidza leadership, practically all of them; also, directors of key enterprises. I recognise the director of the Famos enterprise, the director of the Radio/Television of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza; the director of the hospital, Zica; and some other officials from a neighbouring municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the portion that we just looked at was 1:43.30 to 1:43:53. And if we could move next to the portion of the meeting depicted at 1:55:45.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could commence again at the beginning of Mr. Karadzic's talk, and if the interpreters could translate. I think they have a transcript available to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are determined -- strategic aims which our Assembly adopted, to get separated, and we have separated and formed our state. But some changes have to happen in very Sarajevo in a way that Serbian areas go to Serbs in its entirety, by means of political negotiations and talks, in the way that Serbian city will be formed and separated, as a whole, in the way that the former Sarajevo is transformed into two cities. It is our firm political will and decision, and if our neighbours and the international community as well wish to peacefully solve this problem, then they have to realise that genuine Serbian areas in the territory of Sarajevo have to go to Serbs and a city will be formed there which should have -- be a shelter and home for about 200.000 Serbs, and continually developing on an urban principle and on centre-towards-periphery principle." Could all extra microphones be turned off, please. [Voiceover] "We have a completely clear vision about it, and we will -- try to make it true. We have entirely accepted and welcomed your regulation in the declaration so that the rest of Sarajevo can stay in Republika Srpska if it wants to, as there are economic and historical, national and all other conditions and reasons. And if not, then we will make some arrangements to enable those who do not want to live with us to connect to their territory in some way. "If our neighbours do not show enough understanding, we will decide for ourselves how big Srpsko Sarajevo will be and what will be in Srpsko Sarajevo, and then we -- Sarajevo is a city, and the city in Republika Srpska, because all the land of Sarajevo is situated on Serbian land and all the surroundings are Serbian. And if they do not want to come to a quick solution, the whole of Sarajevo will be Serbian in the end."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let me understand the technical situation at this moment. There was no French translation, obviously. Do you understand the reason why, Mr. Tieger, you or -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You offered the English transcript to the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the sound quality in B/C/S was very, very bad, and we could read the transcript, but we couldn't really hear it all that well, even though the volume was turned up very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The French booth was not able to interpret the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that technical glitch, Your Honour. I would have thought that it would have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, the Bench had no problem in following the English translations. Now I understood the reason why. Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is that one of the meetings at which the -- at which local cadres were reminded by the leadership that the strategic aims were called for, and that the Bosnian Serbs were pursuing the division of Sarajevo into two cities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There were some interruptions, and occasionally I could not hear parts of this speech given by Mr. President Karadzic, and it was with the utmost effort that I could hear some of it. And in answer to your question, I can say, yes, this was a meeting, or, rather, a visit of the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, to the Serbian municipality of Ilidza and partly to the western section of Serbian Sarajevo on the Boxing Day, the second day of Christmas, the 8th of January, 1995, as far as I can determine, in terms of dates. So it was at a moment when the war was already in its final stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The time-frame is until 1:58:28. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, and I'm just checking to see that -- make sure that we've included the first portion, where we -- where Mr. Prstojevic identified himself, and then he also reviewed some of the people in attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to 65 ter 31635, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 31635 is a conversation between Mr. Ristic and yourself, Mr. Prstojevic, on the 16th of June, 1995, and this is a conversation which you had the opportunity to listen to in 2009, when you were interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. Again, we see, at the beginning of the conversation, greetings between yourself and Mr. Ristic. Then there is a discussion about what is -- questions about what is taking place. And as we turn to page 2 of the English, and toward the bottom of your page in B/C/S and moving on to the next page, you say: "All right. We beat the Turks here in Nedzarici. I don't know whether I told you. We beat them here." Ristic says: "You didn't. That's good." You say: "There was an attack over here from two sides, and they went back to Alija not very happy." Ristic says: "Is that right?" You say: "They were beaten, without any results." And then a few lines later, you say: "We pounded them, we attacked them again, and now and then we send over to them a krmaca or two." And "krmaca" there, it says "krmaca," expression for modified air bomb. And Ristic says: "You're right to do so, of course. We need to shake them up a little bit by all means. All in all, I think that things will be okay. I don't know how long you'll be there." First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, can you confirm that you have an opportunity to listen to this conversation, and that you confirmed that this was your voice on the tape?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say in the intercept: "Now and then we send over to them a krmaca," what are you referring to? How often were "krmacas" sent over, and describe what they are.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was having this conversation with the number-one man from the local commune of Vojkovici, in the eastern section, and it was on the second day of the June offensive in the year 1995, when the Muslims were given a green light to launch an attack on the ethnic Serbian areas of Sarajevo with the aim of persecuting and destroying the Serbian population in these areas so that, by military force, it could be taken over, rather than handed over to them peacefully as envisaged by the Dayton Accords. And I wanted to know how serious the attacks were in the eastern part. And I was directly involved in combat on the 15th in the western part, because we knew the date, the hour and the minute when the enemy units would attack us along the entire front-line. And directly in answer to your question, I explained this in detail to your team of investigators in 2009. The team included two military analysts. One of them was Viktor Bezruchenko, who spent the entire war in the Sarajevo area and in the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza. There were also two representatives of OTP. I think that there was a chief Prosecutor and also an interpreter. And it's not exact that the word "krmaca" only implied modified air-bombs, but also all artillery weapons from 82 millimetres, 120, 105, 155 millimetres, and so on. And the word was not invented by Serbs, but rather by the Muslims. All anti-personnel weapons were called "krme" by them, from the small "krme," which is 60 millimetres, that's the simplest mortar shell, to the biggest one. And also as we had 155-millimetre cannon which they used from Igman, we called it "Suta." And I stand by my testimony from 2009 as regards this telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, your testimony in 2009 also embraced a discussion about what you had said to the investigators in 2006, and so let's look at what you're referring to when you use the word "krmaca," and how you explained that. And if we can turn to 65 ter 11562, page 15.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what year is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is the 2006 interview. And you were asked, at --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I referred to my -- to the interview from 2009, because that's the one I remember better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand, and I'll turn your attention to that as well.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this one from 2006 is also not a problem. It's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just so the Court can understand what was said at that time: You were asked about modified air-bombs, that is, bombs designed as gravity bombs that were modified to be used as ground-launched weapons, and then you began to explain. You said: "As the war went on, more hope was laid on some new weapons which will improve and help the defence in this or that way." Then you mention that one such weapon was a tank or an armoured vehicle. And then you continued, on page 16: "Second, for a while, there were stories about 'krmace,' pig-looking-like bombs which were launched in a way towards the enemy units. We were -- we did not have much access to many things, and you don't ask certain things for military protection, just like I never asked about the whereabouts of Karadzic or Mladic, because it would be thought that a secret may be revealed, so if one would ask about the weapons, then the function of it may be revealed. How those 'krmace' bombs existed, and the conversation I had with Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Josipovic of the Serb Sarajevo brigade commander was in most details about it, while awaiting for a meeting between the military and political structures. Among other things, he asked us, Do you know the name of that bomb? Some said this or that. I didn't say anything because I've only heard of its name from soldiers or citizens, whereas he said it is called 'wherever it lands,'" that's from Josipovic in the midst of your quote, "because it was so poor in preciseness that it actually threatened the crew that launched it that it could have landed on the territory and VRS, and not to hit a military target and a civilian one, so once it was in the air, nobody knew how and in what way it would function, so the commanders knew it was extremely imprecise." And then on the next page, 17, you're asked: "During this conversation with Colonel Josipovic, do you recall when that took place?" And you said: "I don't remember, but I remember it was in Vogosca, while waiting for a meeting to take place, round the beginning of 1995 or so, but I think that the Muslim forces were attacking Misici Plateau at the time and coming closer to Vogosca. And what I remembered about it was 'where it lands' was what it was named." And then you refer to the 2009 interview as well. That's 65 ter 22233. And at the page marked "61" in the hard-copy English transcript, but I believe at the bottom of page 81 of the e-court, you confirmed that again, saying: "I remember that in an informal conversation, Josipovic said, 'This weapon is called "wherever it falls," "wherever it lands."' And then the nickname 'krmaca' also applies to an air-bomb because it falls into this category of weapons that I described." Mr. Prstojevic, can you confirm that those are -- accurately captures what you said to the investigators in 2006 and 2009 regarding "krmaca"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you read this from 2006, it does not reflect at all what I said during the interview, because everything is practically wrongly interpreted, maliciously formulated, and the translation is incorrect, and where I say the opposite thing, they interpret it differently. So I completely oppose the idea that this interview of mine from 2006 should be taken as my testimony here today, because everything would have to be checked. I have that in my manuscripts. I also have in translation, in the Serbian language, what I said. And you read it and present it to this Court in such a way and it's translated in such a way that nothing is practically true, except for one thing, and that is that I had heard of this weapon, where I said that, and it was not connected. It was in a group. I did not inquire. I just heard that accidentally while I was in the midst of a discussion and waiting for an official meeting. And as for the interview from 2009, you intentionally left out the portion where I listed all the weapons which they used to call in this or that way. And there are a dozen of places where the word "krmaca" is used where I did not use it, but it's a matter of the interpreter and the investigators and so on. Therefore, I am against taking this as my testimony at the time, even though I do accept what I said when interpreted correctly. But I do not accept that this should be accepted or admitted as a document at this trial. I only accept what I'm saying here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to tender the transcript and the audiotapes of those portions of the interviews that were discussed, and the Court will be free to review those. We have the translation check. As the Court will see, it's a translation that takes place in small chunks as the witness is speaking, but the original tape of the witness's comments and the questions he was asked will be available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness confirmed the statement in 2009, and you stated that in that statement, he embraced his statement in 2006. Could you tell us where he embraced the 2006 statement in his 2009 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
