utterances.text: What I was referring to, Your Honour, was the fact that the 2006 interview was referred to, and then the witness also referred to that same conversation with Josipovic which is referred to in the 2009 interview. That portion begins at -- well, indeed, I'm more than happy to tender the entire part. At the beginning of e-court page 79, I think it is, Mr. Prstojevic is shown the intercept which we've just looked at; that is, the one in which "krmaca" is referred to. And then there's a discussion which goes on about that, and the interviewer points out that in a 2006 interview, Mr. Prstojevic said that one of the nicknames for air-bombs was "krmaca." And then Mr. Prstojevic discusses the Josipovic conversation that was read out. But I'm certainly happy to tender the entirety of that that begins with the presentation of that intercept in 2009, plus, of course, the relevant portions of the 2006 interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we recognise that a prior inconsistent statement can be admissible, and we don't -- we leave it to the Chamber as to how much of it it wishes to receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those parts. So shall we give separate numbers for the two interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 11562 will be Exhibit P2516, and 22233 will be Exhibit P2517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to be precise, could you give the page numbers for the 2009 interview, Mr. Tieger, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the B/C/S page numbers, and I will double-check that, Your Honour, go from B/C/S 79 to B/C/S 82 -- 82, I think. I'm not entirely sure it doesn't bleed over to 83. But I think those references are correct, and we will double-check those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should include the page numbers which the witness alleged have been omitted when you read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I wanted -- I wanted to begin with the moment where he's presented with this intercept, and discussion about "krmaca" begins in that context. And if anyone can show it begins earlier, I'll be happy to tender earlier portions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, could also the recordings be admitted, since the witness has indicated that he was not translated properly? I think it would be proper for the Chamber to also receive the actual recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In relation to the 2006 interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would say 2006 and 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I indicated that that was my intention, and so I certainly have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be done. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could turn next to 65 ter 31673.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I believe you'll recognise this as another intercept that you had an opportunity to listen to in 2009. It's a conversation between you and Mr. Veselinovic on the 29th of June, 1995. It appears, at the beginning, that Veselinovic is trying to reach you, and then you come on the line. And there is a discussion about what's being taking place, referring to counter-attacks and who's been fighting and not. And then, as we continue on to the second page of the English, at the top of the page you say: "That's why we need to reach for this harder and more frequently and ..." And Veselinovic says: "He did that. They mainly didn't move anything that was done, and so ..." And then you say: "Nothing, nothing. The ploughing and the levelling needs to continue further out, the rest ... to be around." Veselinovic agrees: "Yeah, yeah: "You say: "Stay around. I told Radojcic that everything ... all the way to the PTT is ours." He begins say: "Well ..." You say: "And if he attacks, he levels. As I could see on TV, the television's been hit, that's good." And Veselinovic says: "Of course it's good. Mladic congratulated and all." And you say: "Mladic congratulated?" And Veselinovic says: "Sure he did. He called this morning." And then you say -- apparently, there's laughter: "Well, yeah. Oh, bro, it's good, it's good. But we need to use these heavier and stronger if they go into counter-attack and level them out wide." First, Mr. Prstojevic, can you confirm that this is an interview that you had an opportunity to hear in 2009 and confirmed that it was your voice on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've had evidence in this court about what the television building was hit with, but what do you say you were referring to when you say: "We need to use these heavier and stronger," and then there's an object omitted, "if they go into counter-attack"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is a conversation that is taking place during the June offensive in 1995, when we were supposed to be expelled and slaughtered. As opposed to other situations, I was at home, because throughout the war I was away from home, as I am in The Hague now. And I'm talking to a man in the municipality of Ilidza, Mr. Veselinovic. The situation is very difficult, critical, and the chief of staff of the Ilidza Brigade is panic-stricken because the attacks are so forceful and artillery, ammunition and mortar shells are being used with great intensity. We are defending ourselves, and we are practically hitting all military targets. And what I'm saying here, what should be hit, that is my house, Stup 365, before I was born. That's where I spent four or five years, and I know that area. That area, from the home for the elderly in Nedzarici, to the intersection of the railroads from Zenica and Mostar, moved towards Ilidza about 100 metres. That is a military target only. There was one APC next to another, a tank next to another, military units, and other weapons, and there was terrible fighting there. The most important thing for us was that we were persistently in a lowland. Ilidza is below Sarajevo, and our mortars, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think to the extent I sought an answer to my question, I've received all I'm going to get in response to that. I wasn't asking for a dissertation on the entire situation that existed at the time. Your Honour, I'd tender 65 ter 31673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, did you get the answer to your question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I'm not going to press on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what the witness said has not been interpreted. Otherwise, an answer would have been received, the end of the sentence. If you can ask the witness to say what he said at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There were overlapping speakers at that point in time. We cannot hear two people speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prstojevic, could you repeat your last -- the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last part of my answer is as follows: This area that I spoke about is a military target only. When we are speaking about this, I explained very specifically. A 120-millimetre mortar shell is lethal, and that is the heaviest of all. For example, if our artillery were to have 155 millimetres, they still couldn't hit that, because it has to go to the sky and then back down. That's what I mean, that weapon, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As indicated, I tender the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Prstojevic, we've seen that -- your position in the municipality from 1992 through 1995. Is it correct that Mr. Karadzic could have removed you from your position any time he wanted?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. He could not have removed me from that position, because it wasn't President Karadzic who appointed me. I was elected by the Grand Assembly of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza, consisting of about 70 assemblymen on the 5th of April, 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to two -- to portions of two documents. First -- sorry, Your Honour, I have the tape number, but I need the 65 ter number. That's 65 ter 07875, and that would be page 26 of the English and page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look in the middle of the -- sort of the top -- bottom of the top third of the English, you say: "Momcilo Krajisnik and Karadzic could remove me whenever they wanted."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then if we turn to your testimony in the Krajisnik case. At page 14572, you're asked the following: "Q. Let me direct this question, Mr. Prstojevic, to you, in particular. Did Dr. Karadzic, or Mr. Krajisnik, or both, or neither, have the power to remove you whenever they wanted? "A. It is crystal clear. Had he wanted to, had Mr. Karadzic wanted to remove somebody from a position of local authority, he would consult Mr. Krajisnik, and they could do that sort of thing at any time, although I don't know of a single case regarding local authorities such as municipalities." First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, will you confirm that that's what you said during the Krajisnik case, under oath, and also what you said to the interviewers in 2003?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2003, that was a different interview and I couldn't have said that. I'm looking through my notebook now to see what I said during the trial of Mr. Krajisnik. But I could not have said what you read out just now. And I'm looking through my notebook to see what I heard the other day on a CD and what I said with regard to that matter. I will speak up when I find that. As far as I can remember, I said then as well that they could not have removed me because, quite simply, they were not the ones who affected my election as president of the SDS, or the commander of the Crisis Staff, or president of the municipality. Those who elect you can replace you. We were not appointed by way of directives, we, the presidents of municipalities. I'm now looking for this, and we'll see when I find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender those relevant portions, first of the 2003 interview and then of the Krajisnik transcript, which, as I indicated, was page 14572, and those should probably be separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to tender that portion of the Krajisnik transcript separately from the one we have already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it makes much difference, Your Honour. If you think it's more expedient to tender them as one exhibit, that's fine, as long as we have an appropriate reference in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the -- how about the interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this portion of the interview and add the Krajisnik transcript portion to the already-existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P2519.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that concludes my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, can I have the exhibit number of the Krajisnik transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P2513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, although we'll have a break in 15 minutes' time, let us begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I manage to do so, I would like to adhere to the chronology of events, so I would like to ask for 1D1363 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, can you tell us when the Serb Democratic Party was established in Ilidza? There should be a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party in Ilidza was established with a major delay. I was not present at the founding Assembly, so I will have to look up the exact date in my documentation. However, I know for sure that the SDA and the HDZ were established before the SDS in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to this article from "Oslobodjenje," the joint "Oslobodjenje" at that time. The 8th of September, 1990, is the date. Is this piece of news correct? Can you have a look at this, and can you tell us what the essence of this piece of news is?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found my own manuscript. The SDS was established on the 7th of September, 1990. The text I see here is what "Oslobodjenje" carried on the very next day. We can see, from the headline, that it says: "Respect the basis for life together." So that is mutual respect, mutual love, because for love, you need two or three people. And everything is clear, practically, from the headline itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this say that the representatives of the Party of Democratic Action were present as guests?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they were present. I talked to people, and later on as well. I know that Mr. Haris Silajdzic attended in person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please ask the Registry to provide the translation here for all the other participants to see, because there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this first sentence uttered by Momcilo Ceklic, "Brothers and sisters"? Could you read it out, because we haven't much time.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Brothers and sisters, we have met here --" now they've changed this for me, this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, now we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Prstojevic. We can read it now, Mr. Karadzic. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is being highlighted here, in respect of hatred, and, as opposed to hatred, respect for neighbours, brothers and friends, was that the basis upon which the Serb people of Ilidza responded, in terms of joining the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the nature of this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a newspaper report in the joint "Oslobodjenje," two months before the elections, that the Serb Democratic Party was established in Mr. Prstojevic's municipality. The words uttered at the founding Assembly were transmitted here on the basis of what this party is being established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Prstojevic, that then, and all the way up until after the elections, the end of January 1991, the SDA was also in favour of preserving Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a long period of time, up until some Assembly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to other elements, was that the basis for your co-operation with the SDA in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, and mutual respect, maintaining safety and security for all citizens in the municipality of Ilidza, the functioning of the state authorities of government, and that will go on functioning in our territory until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 16197.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that government was shared by the three victorious parties and that, with regard to this power-sharing, the agreement reached at republican level was respected as well as the agreements reached by the local leaderships of the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this agreement reached immediately after the elections, and was it used to usher in the new government after the Communists lost power?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In essence, we had certain objections in respect of the elections. We believed that in Hrasnica I, Hrasnica II, and Sokolovic Kolonija, the Muslims had stolen our votes, or, rather, that they forged the ballots. However, that could not be adopted at the first Assembly, because against us we had Serbs too, assemblymen from the SDP, the reformists, and then the HDZ and so on. But then when that did not succeed, then we proceeded to share power in a very fair way. I think we gave the Croats more than they were entitled to on the basis of the number of votes they had won.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that as for the elections and as for the census in 1991, which was never adopted in the Assembly, there was this strong objection voiced by the Serb side; that is to say, that there were suspicions of forgery, of falsifying the results?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes to both. As for the statistics concerning the elections, I worked on that myself as a mere clerk. And this is how they falsified it: The Serb local communes provided information about the elections, how many people voted and for who. They kept their own information from the local communes that had the largest populations, and then they simply forged a sufficient number of votes for the SDA so that they would get somewhat more than we did. Let me add one more thing. Regardless of that, ethnic Serbs in the SDS and in the reformist party, the SDP, could out-vote both the Muslims and the Croats because they were more numerous. When the census took place, we have written documents through which we challenged the legitimacy of the census in 1991. I know that it was Mr. Momcilo Ceklic, the secretary, who worked on this document, and also Nikola Tausan, an administrative officer who has a degree in law. He worked on this as well. However, this was never presented before the Assembly because, quite simply, the Assembly services that were headed by the president, Mr. Mahmutovic, did not put this on the agenda and there was no debate in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that for the Council of Municipalities, MPs were elected on the basis of major principle, and that in Ilidza, it was the Serb representative that won the majority of votes?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ljubo Bosiljcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that confirm your own suspicions with regard to the census and with regard to the elections, based on the proportion of principle, that something was wrong?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because Mr. Ljubo Bosiljcic could not have become a member of the Republican Assembly if the Muslims were a majority, because the Muslims had their own candidate and the Croats had their own candidate. So most of these divisions were along ethnic lines. So Serbs voted for Bosancic, the Muslims voted for their candidate, and the Croats voted for their candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have to ask you before the kind interpreters who have been exercising restraint, caution us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prstojevic, do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just took off my glasses because I don't really need them now. I just need them when I read. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will have to ask you to pause. We should both pause. I have to remind myself as well, that we should both pause so that we do not exhaust our interpreters. This document that is on the screen now, does it represent a record of the successfully-achieved agreement on responsibility for running the schools in the territory of your municipality? And let us look at the next page now and then the one after that so that we gain sufficient insight. The last one as well, and then let's go back to the first page. Thank you. Can we have the first page now, please. Is it correct, Mr. Prstojevic, that at the proposal of the chairman -- actually, who was chairing this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, this meeting was supposed to be chaired by the president of the SDA, Mahmutovic, or I was supposed to be chairing it. The participants were people who were officials. However, it is under the auspices of the political parties. It wasn't under the auspices of the officials. So it wasn't chairing in terms of the office held. This is an agreement between the political parties, and I'm a participant in this inter-party meeting. And it's not really important, who chaired the meeting. It was probably the representative of the SDA, because it was believed that they were the most numerous party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the first item before this is a proposal to adopt a joint appeal of the victorious parties, addressed to the citizens of Ilidza, and an agreement on specific activities of the victorious parties, in terms of preserving the peaceful co-existence of the citizens of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was done with good reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that on the 23rd of July, 1991, when this meeting was held, there had already been tensions that you consider to be a reason for working further on maintaining co-existence?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was certain information that was coming in from the area of Sarajevo, in more general terms, and that was spilling over to the municipality of Ilidza that is practically on the outskirts, and this disturbed inter-ethnic relations. And we didn't want this kind of spill-over into our area, because the things that the SDA primarily did in the area of the city of Sarajevo, this was leaking into the public domain through people who had a Yugoslav orientation, both Serbs and Muslims and Croats, who were in favour of peace and tolerance. It is the women who transmitted this the best and the most as they had coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a few specific examples of what was going on and what made the citizens of Ilidza feel upset?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see it's almost the end of July 1991. I have specific examples only later. It was only later that they became more prominent. For example, in this period, for instance, this Council for National Defence, for instance, some Muslims established this Council for National Defence that they had, and I cannot remember exactly, but already in one period of time they established some Patriotic League as a separate army. At any rate, these disruptions came from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we remember or do we recall that on the 10th of June or on the 11th of June, this Council for Defence was established by the Muslims, and that this council was chaired by Mr. Izetbegovic, who otherwise, ex officio, was supposed to chair the Council for National Defence of the entire republic, not only the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some meeting at the police building where the creme de la creme of the Muslims was gathered under the chairmanship of Mr. Izetbegovic. Everyone was there, starting with intellectuals to the representatives of the youth. And I fully agree that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, did the Muslim side declare publicly that they would not respond to call-up by the Yugoslav People's Army, and that they would not send conscripts to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, they clearly would appeal to their Muslim citizens not to send recruits to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going on the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, I should have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This time, did you want to say something, or just holding on to your glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. I'm waiting for the break too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This time, the Court Deputy was mistaken, not myself. I should have told you this, Mr. Karadzic: We allotted you 10 hours for your cross-examination. Given that this witness gave his evidence-in-chief viva voce and that the Prosecution has used nine hours and thirteen minutes for its examination-in-chief, I would expect you not to spend more than nine hours, the same amount of time as the Prosecution has used, for your cross-examination. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping I would get more than 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D1388 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting: Mr. Prstojevic, do you know who Senad Sahinpasic, called Saja is? It is not necessary that you know him personally, just if you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him, but I did hear of this man. I don't know. I assume that there's something that has to do with the Patriotic League or the Green Berets in connection with that person. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's see what we have now. Are you familiar with this publication called "Vox"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the "Vox" publication is familiar. I am also aware that there was "Slobodna Bosna." There was another publication similar to "Vox," but I will remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recognise on whose heads is this member of the Handzar Division? Is this person dressed in the traditional way that members of the Handzar Division were dressed, who were members of the SS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "The 4th Reich is coming." We did look at this original publication. All I can tell from this now is we see a soldier, a member of the notorious Handzar Division, that reached Stalingrad in World War II. He's standing, and I can see that he has one foot on your head. I cannot recognise these other people, but evidently it's obvious that they are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could this person next to me be Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot tell from this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we look at the following page, and can the English page stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is October 1991. This publication existed since 1990. Would you agree -- can we just zoom in on the Serbian text, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it states here that: "A year ago, a satirical text appeared in our newspaper about the creation of a hypothetical Islamic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." And so on and so forth? Does that mean that the publication existed from a year before that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this publication, and I remember what this other publication was called too. It was called the "Muslimanski Glasnik." But they are similar and the text in it was similar. It was as if they were written during the war. When you read the text, you feel as if you are not in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time but you feel like you're in some country where there is war. For example, in 1991, Bosnia was occupied. Certain places were occupied. They would be liberated, and so on and so forth. Practically, it was a publication from wartime, even though there was no war at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see here what will happen to the Serbs. First of all, it says: "The day is nearing when the announced Islamic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be proclaimed: That date, which every Muslim in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sandzak is ardently waiting for, has been known for a long time to be the 31st of December of this year." They are thinking of 1990, following the elections, is that correct, since this was published the year before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, that's what I think, yes, but I can't see it here now. But it's quite clear from which period this publication dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to list here in order, and I ask the parties to look at that, all the things that belong to the Serbs or will be given to the Serbs in such an Islamic republic: "Thus, every individual must be aware of the responsibility of the entire people for his uncontrolled actions. Penalties for crimes committed shall be collective - for one destroyed Muslim house, ten Serbian ones will be demolished; for one dead Muslim shall be liquidated 10 to 50 Serbs." Then it says: "All Serbs shall work --" I don't know how many hours per day, probably there is a translation here. Yes, you cannot see it, and: "... their salaries shall be 30 per cent lower. Serbs will be dismissed first. They cannot visit public buildings without special passes. Serbs are getting their food on coupons. Serbs have no national rights. They shall not have any national parties." "And Serbs shall not be deprived of the right to produce alcohol, but Muslims shall be entitled to apply Sharia to all inhabitants of the state." And so on and so forth. Is this a fairly faithful description of the situation of the Christians during the Turkish occupation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I did notice one particular point, and that is that Serbs will be issued food on ration points. And there is a witness who is referring to, Risto Coric. In April 1992, in the neighbourhood of Alipasino Polje, where this person lived, they were already asking for personal ID cards when buying articles in supermarkets and department stores, and that person visited me in Ilidza in April on two occasions. He's a classmate of mine. His hands were shaking as he was telling me about these dramatic things that were happening there. We were powerless to do anything about that. And, secondly, kill 50 for 1, this something that was done in World War II during the fascist period and the fascist NDH state, where for one person killed, 100 Serbs would be shot, they would be taken from their homes and executed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please, in the Serbian. I don't know if it's translated. It's not necessary, because pictures are -- we're looking at pictures. Can we look at this half only where there are photographs? Can we zoom in on that part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is this the usual way of announcing somebody's death, and that these are notices of my own death, the death of Nikola Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, your own deputy, Bosiljcic, the president of the Reformist Party, of Ante Markovic, in Bosnia that was Nenad Kecmanovic, then Nenad Pejic, who was from the Croatian Television?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know all the people in these photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at this part where the text is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is translated, but does it not state here that: "The Homeland War is at our door-step. Bosnia is occupied, but not for long." Is this the title?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to just read one sentence in the last paragraph, the second sentence, and you can control me: "War is our fate. No matter how much weaker we are at this point, we have to get into battle. We have to liberate our Bosnia." Does it not say that in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it states that in the last paragraph that begins: "All right, let's look at the truth straight on."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now zoom in on the bottom part, where we can see who the publisher is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not state here that the founder and publisher is Senad Sahinpasic, editor-in-chief, Esref Rasidagic, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does not the last sentence say "Novi Vox," by a special decision of the republican Committee for Information, does not have to pay a special tax on sales, a special sales tax?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So is this publication favoured as a publication of special national importance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a special magazine that affirms culture, science, music, so it's not common for a political magazine to be waived from paying the sales tax, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 4 from this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, since you overlapped with the interpretation, the interpreters couldn't hear the first part of your previous answer. Did you say anything before you say: "This is a special magazine that affirms culture, science, music ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said this: The "Vox" publication didn't have to pay a sales tax, but I added that it was not usual for political magazines not to have to pay sales tax. This was a privilege for magazines that covered cultural issues, literature, music, that dealt with human values. Such publications did not have to pay a sales tax.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellency, I missed it, I didn't see that, because it turned out that this magazine was affirming culture and music and science and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is a magazine that is actually simulating war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the fourth page from this one. No, no, the fourth page from this one; three more and then the fourth. Can we zoom in on the left part of the page where the photographs are, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the names Hasan Delic and Dzevad Galijasevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzevad Galijasevic, yes. I cannot recall Hasan, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these Muslim names, and are these people Muslims, according to your knowledge and judging by their name?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are Muslim names and these are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not state here: "Stenogram, Chetnik, Hasan and Dzevad"? And does that not mean that these pro-European Muslims were proclaimed Chetniks, just because they were not fundamentalists; in other words, they were proclaimed as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, practically, yes. The magazine that I referred to, the second one, it practically proclaimed all Yugoslav-oriented people, regardless of their ethnicity and religion, enemies of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this publication that I mentioned did that in early May, immediately around the period of the referendum. So it's nothing unusual to see something like this, to see Muslims, who were in favour of tolerance, life together, and who were pro-European and pro-Yugoslav, to find themselves at the brunt of such pressure. They were also fleeing from Muslim areas, and we have data about that in the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the fifth page from this one; that is, three pages from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a photograph of Dr. Mate Mestrovic, a well-known Croatian emigre of the Ustasha orientation; would you agree? Can you please just read out the title to the Trial Chamber? What does Dr. Mate Mestrovic say?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbs are people suffering from complexes."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this publication one of the things that was of concern or causing concern among the Ilidza population?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I quite clearly said that, Mr. President. It simulates war. It writes as if war was already going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so whoever read that had to get upset. But "Slobodna Bosna" also had some extremely disturbing text, as well as another Muslim publication, "Muslimanski Glasnik," which was a bit milder than "Vox," much milder, but, for example, did tag Serbs as enemies of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as other oriented citizens who were in favour of life together and in favour of tolerance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3840 [as interpreted], please, but it should not be broadcast until the Prosecution says whether there are any restrictions about this document. I don't see that there are any, but let us wait. So 1D3480.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Indeed, there are restrictions, and it must be used in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If not broadcasting is not sufficient, then we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let us see it in e-court. Yes, here it is now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, in this text, persons from Sandzak are mentioned as a specific group or entity belonging to Bosnian Muslims. They are also mentioned in the declaration about what lay in wait for the Serbs, and that the Muslims from Sandzak also were in favour of such a state, and that their heart was all for that. Did you have any such phenomenon in your municipality, a phenomenon that could be called the Sandzak Phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we knew from before the war that the Muslims -- the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo, the political and military wing that in late 1991 was already visible, that they had called on the Muslims from Sandzak and Kosovo and Macedonia to participate in the defensive war in Bosnia-Herzegovina which had not yet broken out. However, in Ilidza, the case was rather specific, and so it was in other parts of Sarajevo. There was a marked movement of persons from Sandzak who were moving into one specific local commune, one of the 20 local communes in Ilidza which was called Sokolovic. Because these people from Sandzak were moving in, it received the name Sokolovic Kolonija, which means "Sokolovic Colony." In that area, the persons from Sandzak will become dominant over time, both politically and economically, and they used political and economic influences not only on the Serbs, but also on the Muslims who had lived there originally, and they began to dictate how everything would be ordered in this local commune. One of the prominent people in this local commune was Enver Hodzic - I believe that that was his name - who was nicknamed Enker. These people from Sandzak were a great evil for this local commune and then for Ilidza as well. However, over time they became great evil for Sarajevo, for in Sarajevo the commander-in-chief and the person who organised paramilitary units before the war was Sefer Halilovic, who is himself a native of Sandzak. Up until 1991, he hadn't practically been an inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had been born in Sandzak, in Serbia. And with these people in Sandzak, they will have huge problems, the autochthonous Muslims, who were there from the beginning. And as for us, they were a source of danger as we came into 1992, and there were already incidents in 1992. And immediately after the referendum, there were even some murders of Serbs that were mysterious, and we did not manage to resolve up until the beginning of the war, which broke out on the 3rd of April. So this was a segment of the population which was extremist, fundamentalist, and had at -- had some property that was gained in various unlawful ways from Sandzak all the way to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to ask you as many questions to which you can answer yes or no, though your information is very helpful. Is it true that persons from Sandzak became identified with belligerence, danger and crimes?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that Sokolovic Kolonija became synonymous with building new settlements for the Sandzak Muslims in the Serbian ethnic territories, with the aim of changing the ethnic make-up?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am well aware of this, because since the 1st of February, 1991, I was the secretary for inspection, whose responsibility it was to prevent illegal construction in the area of the entire Ilidza municipality. And, simply, in this period while I was the secretary for inspection, when I introduced the norm for other inspectors, what they had to do on the ground and what had to be prosecuted in court, in this local commune, out of fear, fearing their personal security, the inspectors and Muslim -- both Muslims and Serbs could not do their tasks during 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that illegally-constructed settlements, Sanac and Sokolje, above Rajlovac, were also built in order to allow large numbers of Muslims to move from Sandzak to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you another thing. Would you accept that our language knows terms such as "birth-rate" and "natural birth-rate"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, President, this is something that is well known in science, what is natural birth-rate and what is birth-rate on other bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In English, they have some difficulty with translating this, but let me ask you this: Do you know -- have you seen or heard, and did the people know that even before it was published, that the chief of the religious community of Muslims in Bosnia had issued a fatwa, saying that every Muslim woman should give birth to at least five children so that one could be sacrificed for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this. However, generally speaking, I am aware that according to their religion, because I was born among Muslims 100 kilometres away from Sarajevo, that their religion says that one should give birth to children and should sacrifice oneself, because the one who dies, allegedly, makes revenge. I saw something about that in an instruction for a Muslim soldier from the Meshihat, that is, the Islamic religious community of Zenica. This was published in 50.000 copies, which means that it was available to any and every Muslim soldier. Everything there is founded on the Koran, and I gave a copy of that to investigators in 2003. There are no Geneva Conventions there or other regulations, but how things were done when the Koran was authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will obtain this text, I hope, while you are still testifying and present it. But I wish us to make a distinction between natural birth-rate and the sources of artificial birth-rate. The first source of artificial birth-rate or growth of population, I mentioned the fatwa of the religious leader, that one should give birth to children for political reasons. If you haven't seen it, we'll present it with another witness. Is another source of artificial growth a forced movement of Muslims from Sandzak to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite clear. The moving in of Muslims from Sokolovic Kolonija -- to Sokolovic Kolonija, in Ilidza, it was an artificial means of growth. And it is something that we in Bosnia and Herzegovina were well aware of, that the entire Sarajevo grew in the numbers of the population by people moving in from elsewhere. And natural growth is the birth-rate, the birth-rate of the people who are already inhabitants of one particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard or been informed at party meetings about the secret plan of Omer Behmen and Alija Izetbegovic to provide a third source of artificial growth of population; that up to four million Muslims should move into Bosnia, mainly Turks?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. However, I know that Behmen is one of the authors of "The Islamic Declaration," together with Mr. Izetbegovic. However, it wasn't only Turkey, Mr. President; it was generally known. All of us knew that Islamic fanatics find closer to their hearts a man from Asia, Africa, wherever, just as long as they are of the Islamic faith, rather than their very own neighbours next to whom they live. In wartime, they were counting on having people moved in from these countries. They were not trying to save their own lives. They didn't mind how many of their soldiers would lose their lives when fighting the Serbs. Before the war and even now, they will increase their population that way, unless the European Union brings this to a halt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to see what the Serbs were doing at the same time. Could we have 65 ter 30407 now, please. This is an intercept, a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Jovo Jovanovic, the 6th of November, 1991, before our plebiscite on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who Jovo Jovanovic is?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovo Jovanovic is an elderly man, if I can put it that way, the president of the City Board of the SDS, and a man who, in contrast to many Serbs, myself included, is a person whose ancestors have lived in the territory of Sarajevo since time immemorial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please have a look at this intercept. I called him late in the evening, and I apologised. So everyone will have an opportunity to see this document: It has to do with preparations for our referendum on the 10th and 11th of November; isn't that right? That's when we had our plebiscite on whether we wished to remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that you even went to some of the polling station in Ilidza. And that Enker who I mention here recorded you with a video camera in Sokolovic Kolonija, if I remember properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly, thank you. Can we have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it is. Jovo Jovanovic says: "In the morning, I will be speaking about the plebiscite on the radio." It's around the middle of the page in Serbian: [In English] "Tomorrow morning, I will be on Radio 202 at 10 to 7.00." [Interpretation] "10 to 7.00." And this is what I say: "Aha." And then in a peaceful way, we are just expressing our views. And Jovo says: "You know what it's like, strong current." And I say: "Yes, yes, and that's great. Everybody should come out." And Jovo says: "Of course." And I say: "That's the best way to maintain the peace." And so on. Then Jovo says: "It's going pretty well." And Radovan: "All right, Jovo, take care." Jovo: "Have a nice day, so goodbye." And another: "Goodbye." Is this fully in line with what you know about our efforts to work on a political level while preserving togetherness and unity?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this and on the basis of what you, yourself know, is it not the case that this referendum was only there to express the wish of the people, and that no decision is derived from it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the referendum was fully public, and other people who were not only Serbs, who were of a pro-Yugoslav orientation, Muslims included, those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs as well, they all voted in the referendum, and there is information to that effect in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? MFI'd, rather, because of our reservations, in general, vis-a-vis intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Prstojevic, that the Muslim political party establishes crisis staffs at a very early stage, and that even the Presidency, in September 1991, established a crisis staff, and in this way basically handed over all power to Ejub Ganic ?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Crisis Staff of the SDA for Bosnia-Herzegovina was established even before that, Mr. President, around the middle of the year, practically, because the Crisis Staff for Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica -- or, rather, for Ilidza, the Muslim part, was established already in August -- July, August, somewhere around that time. So these republican and regional crisis staffs must have been established before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Serb Crisis Staff in Ilidza; when was that established?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a document about that, so we'll get to that topic too, but let us distinguish between crisis staffs that belonged to municipalities and those that belonged to political parties. Could I now please have 65 ter 10765 [as interpreted]. Chronologically, I am going back to this, because it will be easier for us to show what you know from that time in such a way. 10756 would be the 65 ter number. We have Vogosca, but we need Ilidza. No, no, the City Board, yes. On this page, in Serbian, do you see that this is the 10th joint session of the City Board and the Executive Board of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the 27th of November, 1991. And there is a reference down here to Mr. Jovo Jovanovic as president, and you identified him as the president a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 6. I believe that it's page 6 in English as well. Maybe it's 5. Please, could we have a look. It starts -- oh, it's okay, it seems to be okay. No, no. In Serbian, keep this one -- both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the top in Serbian: "Jovo Jovanovic responded that it was correct that in the municipality of Stari Grad, the Serb people had no rights and that they do not take part in executive power, and that there is out-voting in Parliament. However, all of that is coming to the fore in other municipalities as well, where we are minority people, such as Hadzici, Novi Grad, Trnovo and so on, because the other parties in the coalitions out-voted the Serb representatives in the Parliament and in the executive government and made the decisions instead of them." Because of this, he stated: "Very soon, regionalisation will be carried out, and in areas where the Serb majority and places were Serbs were owners of real estate, Serb organs of government will be formed." Is this in line with your own experience about how the Serb people fared after this government was formed, after these first elections?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was supposed to participate in this session of the City Board because I was a member of the City Board. I cannot remember whether I was present or not. However, it is fully correct, what Mr. Jovo Jovanovic is saying here at the top of the page. That is the truth, and nothing but the truth. In part, this goes for Ilidza as well. Efforts will be made to out-vote us, especially in the Executive Board, where I was a member, too; in the municipal government, that is. If the Croats were to go hand in hand with the Muslims, we would regularly be out-voted. However, we were fortunate enough, in so much as that the Croats did not always want to go hand in hand with the Muslims. But these two first points made here in this text are the truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have the next page in Serbian, and in English we can keep this page. You can just scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Jovo Jovanovic said that the SDA, itself, was facing problems with Hadzibajric and other extremists in the SDA. Jovo Jovanovic made the proposal that full assistance should be given to the construction of the first church in the city of Sarajevo, on Veljine, by both the municipal boards, by engaging --" and here it says "decision." That is to say, the construction of the first Orthodox Church in Veljine is given assistance of 50.000 dinars. Is this to say this was the first Serbian Orthodox Church that was built in Sarajevo since the end of the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, the construction started before the war. And it is in the territory of the municipality of Novi Grad, and during the war, it was in the territory of the municipality of Ilidza. I am quite familiar with the problems that were involved in getting permission for this church. Perhaps it's a kilometre and a half away from my house. There were so many obstructions that were placed before it by the Communist government. As a matter of fact, the railways of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and I was among the 7.000 employees there at the time, I was the number-three man. The priest asked me to get a document from him -- for him certifying that no railroad would go through that area where that location is, and I managed to get that document for him. So this is the first church whose construction started between the two wars, between 1945 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this Hadzibajric, who Jovo calls an extremist, is a person with whom the Muslims have problems as well, was the president of the municipality of Stari Grad, where the Serbs had no rights?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Serbs had problems there. But believe it or not, I do not remember who the president over there was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 17422.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: The distinguished Mr. Tieger asked you about that speech of mine in Ilidza, whether I was advocating the division of Sarajevo. That was already the end of the war, 1995. Do you agree that I am not mentioning division at all there; I am referring to transformation? If necessary, we can call this document up.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other day, I listened quite carefully to that speech, and this was my understanding: Because it was obvious that the war was coming to an end, because at this hospital that you visited at the time, you visited part of the Famos factory, then the Zica Hospital, the radio/television, Ilidza and so on, there were no wounded persons, it was my understanding that you say at one point in time, If we do not reach agreement, then it is with pleasure that we are going to do such and such a thing, as if we would get a present. I understand that as something said by way of a joke for the sake of optimism among the people, that something nice should be said to the people who are present there so that they could have a bit of a laugh too. And as far as I can see, they are accepting what it is that you were explaining there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 40 of today's transcript, it says that I said that through negotiations, by peaceful means, we shall attain the transformation of Sarajevo into two cities. Do you remember that the beginning of regionalisation was based -- even before the war, when people thought that there would be no war, it was based on the idea that Serbs should run Serb affairs, and Muslims should run Muslim affairs, and that for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and for Sarajevo, our position was transformation, not division?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that before the war and even during the negotiations that took place during the course of the war, itself, we mentioned the model of Brussels, where, out of 17 municipalities, each and every one belongs to either the Walloons or the Flemish, but the city is not divided physically, but only in administrative terms?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's hard to remember all of that. I know that the model of Switzerland was mentioned as well, cantonisation. And I have to say something else here. Then and now, the Serbs considered Bosnia-Herzegovina to be their own state. That is our state, and we never challenged it, we never denied it. And in that state, people were always supposed to live in a neighbourly way, and everybody was supposed to run their own affairs. And, of course, it is quite clear that above that, there is state authority, some kind of joint authority. The basic model was always, as far as I know, joint authority, joint government. And as you go further down towards the bottom, everything is brought to the ethnic communities, the Serbs, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at what we have on the screen. I don't know if it's "Wednesday, the 15th of January, 1992." And in this Gazette of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It gives a recommendation on the establishment of municipal assemblies of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you please read the first two paragraphs? Perhaps you can read them out loud, because I don't know why there is no translation. Perhaps there is a translation. Can you please read them out loud?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the "21st of November, 1991" here, "The president of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BiH," "Momcilo Krajisnik," "Master's degree." What am I supposed to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there is a translation. This belongs to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can read: "On the basis of the proposal of the Executive Board --" Or should I just read the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Full support is given to the Yugoslav People's Army in the defence of the joint state of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the question. The speakers were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible to follow at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We overlap, yes. I believe the Prosecution has a translation, because they obtained this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Unless it has been already translated, it's for you to translate this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I just ask for the recommendation, where it says: "The Deputies' Clubs recommended"? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could do that. But my microphone is not adjusted very well, so then I'm speaking completely off microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause before you start answering the question. So when you start answering the question, while we are hearing the interpretation, it's impossible for the interpreters to interpret what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I am going try to do it so that we can do it more quickly. The Deputies' Clubs of the Serbian Democratic Party in the municipal assemblies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where decisions are imposed by over-voting that are counter to the interests of the Serbian people, are asked to contribute or to adopt decisions on the founding of municipal assemblies of the Serbian people. The municipal assemblies of the Serbian people would comprise deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party and other deputies of Serb ethnicity who state -- who give a statement on joining the Assembly. Now I'm going to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Through quite extraordinary efforts that continue to astound me, Mr. Reid has found a translation. I reiterate, these things can be found in advance by the Defence, but if it's helpful now, he can call that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. In the meantime, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first question about this, Mr. Prstojevic, is this: Do you agree that the Serbs first declared some bodies which would not function until it turned out that there was no other option? Does this recommendation mean that some -- the existence of some Serbian Assembly should just be proclaimed, but that the work in the joint body still continues?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was that the case with your own Crisis Staff, for example, which was just declared in early 1991 and became active only when the war broke out as the Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the distribution of municipalities in Sarajevo was different and that Rajlovac was a Serbian Assembly -- a Serbian municipality up until 1957?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but other Serb neighbourhoods also were municipalities up until that year; for example, Blazuj, which was part of Ilidza and which was a local community within Ilidza, used to be a municipality. I'm aware of this also in the case of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that from that year or those years, a sort of engineering began whereby Serbian municipalities were merged in order to turn them from majority ones into minority ones? For example, the Hadzici municipality, which was a Serbian majority, was joined on to the Tarcin and other communities, thereby creating a Serb minority?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct in the case of Tarcin and Hadzici. I know very well the case of Hadzici, because in 1972 to 1975, I lived in that municipality and my wife hails from there. Centar is exclusively a Serbian area, but then by creating new parts of the new municipality, it became a majority Muslim-populated area. In the town of Sarajevo, there is a striking example with the formation of the municipality Novi Grad, which will then take parts of the Novo Sarajevo and the Ilidza municipalities, and in that way create a change in the ethnic composition of the Ilidza municipality as well as the Novo Sarajevo municipality. In that municipality, there were 37.000 Serbs, which means that that is the highest number of Serbs in any municipality, but it was incorporated in such a way that Serbs made up only 30 per cent of the overall population of that municipality. They will experience catastrophe in the war, and we will get 3.000 Serbs in the municipality of Rajlovac who ended up under our control, under our authority. And then we would also have some parts that Ilidza took under its wing immediately at the beginning of the war, i.e., Nedzarici, where the Serbs were an absolute majority, and then later -- or, actually, immediately parts of Dobrinja, the people who had been living there for ages, whose land was used to create the municipality of Dobrinja --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not complete his thought.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now find the translation in the e-court for the Trial Chamber for this document, for this excerpt from the "Official Gazette"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you can read the transcript, Mr. Karadzic, check whether the -- what the witness has said has been fully translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it your point that these traditional Serbian areas were used to erect new settlements for the purpose of changing the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also of new territorial organisations. That was also an objective. And that is why I referred to the creation of the municipality of Novi Grad - I don't know which year that occurred - where the ethnic structure in Ilidza and Novo Sarajevo was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the following page, please. Yes, this is the recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this recommendation mean that something can happen, but does not necessarily have to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am now going to ask you about the so-called Variant A and B paper. Can we call up the first page. It wouldn't be a bad idea. This is 65 ter 00219. Do you agree or do you remember that all official documents of the Serbian Democratic Party must and did have a register number at the top, as well as the date, and on the last page they bore the signature of the authorised person?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we bring back the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there is no number here, this register number? There is a date at the bottom, but this document does not have a record number, register number?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, it doesn't have one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the one page but last. Then the last page, then, because obviously something is attached here that I am counting as a page. The last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you notice that it states, on the first page "The Main Board," but at the end it states "Crisis Staff," and there is no signature or any particular name given?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this look to you like some draft or some proposal that would need to be completed by reviewing it and adopting it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know what it looks like, because these are completely two different bodies involved. At the heading, there is one body. At the end, where the signatory should be, is another body. So it's inconceivable that this can happen on any kind of normative act of any party or of any institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a reserve officer, do you recognise elements of military intelligence, of military mentality, where a crisis staff commander is referred to and so on and so forth? Is this something that is completely different to you from everything that the Serbian Democratic Party stood for?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already said that a number of times. When I was a director at my enterprise, there was a committee for ONO and DSZ, so -- All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. These bodies existed in municipalities and also in towns, so the number-one person would always be the director or the president of the municipality. I always would see the same thing there. During socialism, a committee would be referred to, and here we have the Crisis Staff, and everything was done on the basis of a book. I have it here with me. It's a wartime book that is riddled with bullets. I can bring it tomorrow. And it deals with the strategy of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. This is a red book, and it regulates all of these matters. This is my book that I had before the war and during the war. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to say that this text was adopted by a group of frightened officers, who saw that they could come to harm because they had become hated, and it was distributed without any kind of review or adoption, would that sound reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm going to remind you about something here. That Muslim publication that I mentioned - I remember the date now too - it's from the 3rd of March, 1992, it mentioned all JNA officers which did not sign loyalty to the Muslim leadership through any channel as enemies of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I agree with you completely, and I said on a number of occasions that this document was not reviewed at the meeting which I attended. There was no mention of it at all, but somebody gave it to someone of those people from Ilidza who were there. Had they given it to me, I would have known about it. But in time, it also came into my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you were not at that meeting, you cannot know the number. But would it be acceptable to you that members of the Main Staff, the Executive Staff, and representatives of a number of municipalities were there, meaning that there were several hundred people there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President, I was at that meeting. And do you know how I know that there were more than 500 people there?
